classification_signals: Abstract states: 'This paper presents an evaluation of the tools with professionals and students.' (p. 1)
Methodology described in 'Usability Study' section (p. 5), detailing participant recruitment (professionals, students) and experimental design (design assignments, tool order, questionnaires).
Results presented quantitatively in tables (e.g., Table 7, 8, 9, 10, 11) and qualitatively in sections like 'Performance of the Tools', 'Ease of Use', 'Creativity' (p. 7-11).
Discussion section interprets the empirical findings and provides recommendations based on the evaluation (p. 12-13).
title: Materials in Products Selection: Tools for Including User-Interaction in Materials Selection
authors: I. E. H. van Kesteren et al., 2007

limitations: Participants used the tools without any preparation, which might not reflect real-world usage where designers would prepare.
The picture cards and their associated personality terms may vary depending on culture, trends, and time, potentially limiting generalizability.
The existing material sample sets from suppliers were too detailed for the initial defining phase, and the number of samples was limited by practical issues (storage, transport).
There was variation in participants' opinions regarding the tools' inspiring qualities, making it hard to definitively state if creativity was improved or restricted for all.
Not every tool consistently directed to a material profile described in sensorial properties, with picture and sample tools often remaining at the perceptual level.
Students, lacking experience with client projects and design brief meetings, reacted differently to the tools, finding them more restricting and harder to use than professionals.
The study suggests that no single tool suits all users, indicating individual differences in preference and effectiveness.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study evaluates the Materials in Products Selection (MiPS) tools, designed to help product designers and clients define sensorial material properties for desired user-interaction. The tools, comprising picture cards, material samples, and a question tool, were tested with professionals and students. Key findings indicate that the tools generally increase certainty and consensus in defining material properties, with the picture tool being the most usable and inspiring, though it can limit 'out-of-the-box' thinking. The question tool effectively directs discussions towards sensorial properties but was found less inspiring and harder to use. Professionals found the tools stimulating for creativity, while students often perceived them as restrictive. The study concludes that a combined approach, emphasizing a clear 'converging step' to translate perceptual terms into sensorial properties, is most effective, and recommends tailoring tools to professional designers. Limitations include the lack of participant preparation, cultural specificity of examples, and the observation that no single tool is universally optimal.
